elements.element: Customer may assign without Vendor consent to an affiliate.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without MSL's consent to any entity controlling, controlled by or under common control with IBM.

elements.element: Customer may assign without Vendor consent to a successor in a merger.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without consent to a successor in interest by way of merger.

elements.element: Customer may assign without Vendor consent to a successor in an acquisition.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without consent to a successor in interest by way of acquisition.

elements.element: Customer may assign without Vendor consent to a successor in a sale of substantially all assets.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without consent to a successor in a sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.

elements.element: Vendor may assign only with Customer consent.
elements.evidence: The clause repeatedly requires IBM's prior written approval for MSL assignments, including assignments to an MSL Related Company.

elements.element: Customer consent to a Vendor assignment may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: The opening sentence provides that the other Party's approval may not be unreasonably withheld or delayed, and the MSL Related Company provision applies the same standard expressly.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor prohibition appears. IBM could consent to an MSL assignment to an IBM competitor.

elements.element: Vendor has no termination right arising from Customer change of control.
elements.evidence: The clause grants MSL no such termination right and expressly states that IBM's listed successor transactions, including acquisition and reorganization, give MSL no right to terminate.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor without Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without MSL's consent to a successor in interest through merger, acquisition, reorganization, or sale of the relevant assets or business.

elements.element: Customer must provide Vendor written notice of an assignment to a successor.
elements.evidence: IBM's successor assignment right is expressly conditioned on written notice to MSL.

elements.element: Vendor may assign to a successor without Customer consent.
elements.evidence: The MSL sale-and-merger provision requires notice and successor assumption but does not waive IBM consent; the clause separately states that MSL may not assign or transfer without IBM's prior written approval.

elements.element: Vendor must provide Customer written notice of an assignment to a successor.
elements.evidence: MSL must immediately notify IBM of specified sale, merger, or ownership-transfer decisions, but the operative language does not require that notice to be written.

elements.element: Customer assignments other than to a successor require Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: Except for the express affiliate and successor carve-outs, IBM remains subject to the opening requirement for the other Party's prior written approval.

elements.element: Vendor consent to Customer assignments other than to a successor may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: The opening sentence states that the required approval may not be unreasonably withheld or delayed.

elements.element: Vendor assignments other than to a successor require Customer consent.
elements.evidence: MSL assignments remain subject to IBM's prior written approval, including under the general restriction and the specific MSL provisions.

elements.element: Customer consent to Vendor assignments other than to a successor may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: The opening approval standard applies to either Party and is not expressly displaced by the later, duplicative MSL approval requirement.

result.reason: The preferred position fails because there is no absolute prohibition on assignment by MSL to an IBM competitor. The fallback fails because MSL receives no clear right to assign to a successor without consent and its notice duty is not expressly written. The redline is not minimal: it also changes the consent standard for subcontracting and adds suspension and repricing protections beyond either position. That unrelated subcontracting change prevents full preservation of the original commercial intent. Drafting is further weakened by duplicative MSL restrictions and the incomplete fragment “MSL shall”.
